title: India Emerges as Asia's 'Anti-AI' Trade as Global Tech Rally Cools
excerpt: Foreign investors are rotating into Indian equities after a brutal first half, drawn by diversified earnings and the implosion of concentrated semiconductor bets in South Korea and Taiwan.
body:
• As global AI stocks stumble, India's benchmark index has climbed 5% since mid-June, drawing foreign capital away from tech-heavy South Korea and Taiwan.
  • Foreign investors bought more than $1.6 billion of Indian equities in July, reversing months of outflows that saw $29 billion leave in the first half of 2026.
  • HSBC, UBS, Goldman Sachs, and Bernstein have all upgraded or flagged India as a buy, citing improving earnings and attractive valuations outside tech.
  • India's lack of pure-play AI stocks — once seen as a weakness — is now a hedge against the concentrated risks battering semiconductor markets.

The Rotation

For the better part of two years, India was the market nobody wanted. While South Korea and Taiwan rode a historic semiconductor boom — their benchmark indices surging roughly 90% and 80% respectively over the past 12 months — India's Sensex drifted down about 5%, starved of the AI-fueled capital that was transforming Asian markets.

That calculus has shifted sharply this summer. Since mid-June, equities in South Korea and Taiwan have stumbled as investors question the durability and profitability of massive AI capital expenditure. India, meanwhile, has quietly climbed 5%, emerging as what Reuters columnist Siddharth Raychaudhuri calls Asia's ultimate "anti-AI" trade.

"India could emerge as one of the few markets where growth remains sustainable compared with the rest of the world."

— Mayuresh Joshi, Head of Equity Research, India, William O'Neil & Company

The Money Is Following

The rotation is more than theoretical. Foreign investors bought more than $1.6 billion worth of Indian equities in July — modest in absolute terms, but a stark reversal after roughly $29 billion in outflows during the first six months of the year, according to NSDL data.

The institutional upgrades have come fast. Over the past month, HSBC raised India to "neutral" from "underweight," while UBS upgraded its rating to "attractive" from "neutral." Goldman Sachs and Bernstein have both flagged the prospect of a second-half rebound for the Nifty 50.

Ji Young Park, senior Asia ex-Japan equity portfolio manager at Amundi, which manages $2.8 trillion in assets, said the firm was "constructive" on India as concerns over high oil prices were largely reflected in valuations. Park expects AI-driven rotation into India to persist as valuations in sectors such as financials, healthcare, and industrials have become attractive.

Why India Is Different

India's public markets offer few pure-play AI stocks. Its IT giants — Infosys, TCS, Wipro — remain anchored in cost-efficient services rather than chip design or AI model building. For months, that left global allocators uninterested.

Now that same gap looks like a feature. When SK Hynix, South Korea's AI-era darling, reported a sixfold jump in quarterly profit but still failed to stem market panic because results lagged expectations, the concentrated risk embedded in semiconductor-heavy markets became impossible to ignore.

India's diversified earnings base — spanning financials, healthcare, consumer goods, and manufacturing — offers a fundamentally different risk profile. Improving domestic consumption, a stabilizing rupee backed by RBI swap facilities, and a maturing capital market infrastructure give global allocators multiple entry points beyond a single sector bet.

Not Quite Anti-AI After All

The "anti-AI" label may itself be temporary. India is finding its own place in the AI ecosystem — not in hardware, but in services, implementation, and digital infrastructure. The government's push for data center construction, digital payments through UPI, and its semiconductor incentive program suggest the country is positioning itself as an AI deployment market rather than an AI creation one.

For now, though, the trade is straightforward. As one William Blair analyst put it, Indian corporate earnings are moving "onto an upward trajectory" after slowing through 2024 and 2025. Whether the rotation proves durable will depend on two factors: a sustained earnings recovery after several lacklustre quarters, and a de-escalation of Middle East tensions that have kept oil prices elevated.

"India is set up for a strong second half of the year," said William Blair's McClone. The question is whether global capital agrees long enough to make it stick.
